title: Desert, oasis and Bedouin life
summary: Deserts cover a large part of the Arab world, from the Sahara in North Africa to the Empty Quarter of Arabia. Meet the oasis and its date palms, the camel, the goat-hair tent and the old customs of hospitality, and see how most people of Bedouin descent live today. Key word: صَحْرَاء (desert).

sections.title: Seas of sand and rock

photo.alt: Long, rippled sand dunes in soft evening light stretching to the horizon in the Rub' al-Khali in Oman.
photo.caption: Dunes of the Empty Quarter, الرُّبْعُ الْخَالِي, in Oman.

body: The Arabic word for desert is صَحْرَاء, and the English name 'Sahara' comes from it. The Sahara stretches across North Africa, from Egypt and Libya to Algeria, Morocco and Mauritania. On the Arabian Peninsula lies the Rub' al-Khali, الرُّبْعُ الْخَالِي ('the empty quarter'), one of the largest sand deserts in the world. It is shared by Saudi Arabia, Oman, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen, and some of its dunes, each a كَثِيب (plural kuthbān), are more than 200 metres high.

Not every desert is a sea of sand. Wadi Rum, وَادِي رَمّ, in the south of Jordan is a wide valley of red sand between huge mountains of sandstone and granite. The word wādī means a valley or a dry riverbed that can suddenly fill with water after rare heavy rain. Other deserts are flat plains of gravel and stone. Wadi Rum is a protected area and a UNESCO World Heritage site, and today it is also one of Jordan's best-known places for visitors.

Desert weather is extreme. The days can be very hot, حَارّ, and in summer, صَيْف, the temperature in the shade often goes above 40 degrees. Dry air keeps little heat, so after sunset the desert cools quickly and the nights can be cold, بَارِد. In winter, شِتَاء, nights in some deserts come close to freezing. People who know the desert carry plenty of water, مَاء, a scarf against the sun and the sand, and something warm for the night.

sections.title: The oasis and the date palm

photo.alt: A still lake reflecting a long line of date palms and a few low mud-brick buildings under a cloudy sky at Siwa Oasis, Egypt.
photo.caption: Palm groves beside a lake at Siwa Oasis, سِيوَة, in Egypt's Western Desert.

body: An oasis, وَاحَة, is a place in the desert where water comes to the surface from springs or wells, so that trees and crops can grow and people can live. Siwa, سِيوَة, in Egypt's Western Desert not far from the Libyan border, is famous for its many springs, its salt lakes and its large groves of date palms and olive trees. Many people in Siwa speak a Berber (Amazigh) language called Siwi at home, as well as Arabic.

Al-Ahsa, الْأَحْسَاء, in the east of Saudi Arabia, is one of the largest oases in the world, with well over two million date palms, old springs and canals. In 2018 UNESCO listed the Al-Ahsa Oasis as a World Heritage site. Like many oases, it is not a small green island but a whole region of farms, villages and towns, and its city of Hofuf is a busy modern centre.

The date palm, نَخْلَة (plural nakhīl), was for centuries the most useful tree of the desert. Its fruit, تَمْر (dates), keeps for a long time and gives a lot of energy, and its trunk, leaves and fibre were used for roofs, mats, baskets and rope. Today dates are still offered to guests with coffee in many homes, and many people eat a date to break the fast in Ramadan.

sections.title: Camels, tents and guests

photo.alt: Black tents with white stripes standing on red sand below pale sandstone cliffs at a visitors' camp in Wadi Rum, Jordan.
photo.caption: Tents in the style of the black goat-hair tent at a visitors' camp in Wadi Rum.

body: For thousands of years the camel, جَمَل, carried people, goods and water across the desert and gave milk, meat, hair and leather. A female camel is a نَاقَة, and camels as a group are إِبِل. Classical Arabic has many more camel words, for camels of different ages, colours and uses, and early dictionary writers collected dozens of them. The popular claim of 'a thousand words for camel' is an exaggeration, and most of these words are rare today. Camel racing and camel beauty contests are still popular in the Gulf.

The traditional tent of the Bedouin is called بَيْتُ الشَّعْر ('house of hair'), because its cloth is woven from black goat hair, traditionally by the women of the family. In the heat the loose weave gives shade and lets air pass; in rain the hair fibres swell and keep most of the water out. A woven curtain divides the tent into a part for receiving guests and a part for the family. Careful: shaʿr (with a) is hair, while شِعْر (with i) is poetry.

Hospitality, ضِيَافَة, and generosity (karam) are central values of desert life. A guest, ضَيْف, is welcomed with Arabic coffee, قَهْوَة, often flavoured with cardamom and served in small cups, together with dates. In many tribes an old custom says that a guest may stay three days before being asked about his business. In 2015 Arabic coffee, as a symbol of generosity, was added to UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage, nominated by Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Oman and Qatar.

sentences.en: A nāqa is a female camel.
sentences.literal: the she-camel (is the) female (of) the camel

sentences.ar: بَيْتُ الشَّعْرِ مَصْنُوعٌ مِنْ شَعْرِ الْمَاعِز.

mistakes.why: With a (shaʿr) the word means hair, so the goat-hair tent is bayt ash-shaʿr. With i (shiʿr) it means poetry, and bayt shiʿr is a line of poetry.

sections.title: Stars, poetry and Bedouin life today
body: Far from city lights, the night sky over the desert is full of stars. A star is a نَجْم (plural nujūm). Travellers and caravans used the stars to find their way, and the rising of certain stars marked the seasons: in Arabia, the first appearance of the star Canopus (suhayl) before dawn is still taken as a sign that the worst summer heat is ending. Many star names used in astronomy today come from Arabic, for example Aldebaran (ad-dabarān, 'the follower') and Altair (aṭ-ṭāʾir, 'the flying one').

Poetry, شِعْر, has long been the great art of Arabia. The most famous early Arabic poems, the long odes known as the Muʿallaqāt, often begin with the poet stopping at an empty campsite where his loved one once lived. Poetry is still very much alive: Nabati poetry, composed in the spoken dialects of the Arabian Peninsula, fills television competitions such as 'Million's Poet' in Abu Dhabi, and poems are recited at weddings and family gatherings.

The word بَدْو (Bedouin) is related to bādiya, the open desert land; settled people of towns and villages are called ḥaḍar. Today most people of Bedouin descent live settled lives in towns and cities and work as teachers, engineers, soldiers, drivers, business people or in tourism. Many keep their dialect, family ties, poetry and customs of hospitality, and some families still keep camels or sheep or spend weekends in the desert in the cool season, usually arriving by car. In Wadi Rum, many local Bedouin work as guides and run camps for visitors.

words.note: Feminine. The Sahara is often called aṣ-ṣaḥrāʾ al-kubrā, 'the great desert'.
Plural kuthbān. In everyday speech many people simply say 'a hill of sand'.
One tree; palm trees together are nakhīl.
A collective noun: one date is tamra.
From the same root as ضَيْف (guest).
Do not confuse with shaʿr, hair.
One Bedouin man is badawī; the English word Bedouin comes from the same root.

reading.title: A trip to the oasis
reading.ar: سَافَرْتُ مَعَ صَدِيقَتِي إِلَى وَاحَةِ سِيوَة فِي غَرْبِ مِصْر. فِي الطَّرِيقِ رَأَيْنَا صَحْرَاءَ وَاسِعَةً وَكُثْبَانًا عَالِيَة. فِي الْوَاحَةِ عُيُونُ مَاءٍ وَنَخِيلٌ كَثِير. كَانَ النَّهَارُ حَارًّا، وَلٰكِنَّ اللَّيْلَ كَانَ بَارِدًا جِدًّا. فِي الْمَسَاءِ شَرِبْنَا الشَّايَ مَعَ عَائِلَةٍ مِنْ سِيوَة، وَأَكَلْنَا التَّمْر. بَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ نَظَرْنَا إِلَى النُّجُومِ فِي السَّمَاء. فِي السَّنَةِ الْقَادِمَةِ نُرِيدُ أَنْ نَزُورَ الْأَحْسَاء.
reading.en: I travelled with my friend to Siwa Oasis in the west of Egypt. On the way we saw a wide desert and high dunes. In the oasis there are springs of water and many palm trees. The day was hot, but the night was very cold. In the evening we drank tea with a family from Siwa and ate dates. After that we looked at the stars in the sky. Next year we want to visit Al-Ahsa.
segs: Al-Ahsa (an oasis region in Saudi Arabia)

options: in the east of Saudi Arabia
readingQuestions.explain: The text says وَاحَةِ سِيوَة فِي غَرْبِ مِصْر: Siwa Oasis in the west of Egypt.
اللَّيْلَ كَانَ بَارِدًا جِدًّا: the night was very cold, although the day was hot.

readingQuestions.prompt: Which place do they want to visit next year?
readingQuestions.explain: نُرِيدُ أَنْ نَزُورَ الْأَحْسَاء: we want to visit Al-Ahsa, the big oasis in Saudi Arabia.

quiz.explain: صَحْرَاء is a desert; the English name 'Sahara' comes from it.

quiz.prompt: Which desert is shared by Saudi Arabia, Oman, the UAE and Yemen?
quiz.explain: الرُّبْعُ الْخَالِي, the Empty Quarter, covers the south of the Arabian Peninsula.

quiz.prompt: Why is the Bedouin tent called بَيْتُ الشَّعْر?
options: its cloth is woven from goat hair
it is made of palm leaves
quiz.explain: shaʿr (with a) is hair: the tent is woven from black goat hair. شِعْر (with i) is poetry.
النَّاقَةُ أُنْثَى الْجَمَل: a nāqa is a female camel. Camels as a group are إِبِل.

quiz.prompt: The desert is hot in the daytime. What are desert nights often like?
quiz.explain: Dry air keeps little heat, so the desert cools quickly after sunset: الصَّحْرَاءُ حَارَّةٌ فِي النَّهَارِ وَبَارِدَةٌ فِي اللَّيْل.

quiz.prompt: How do most people of Bedouin descent live today?
options: moving with their camels all year
quiz.explain: يَسْكُنُ أَكْثَرُ الْبَدْوِ الْيَوْمَ فِي الْمُدُن: most live settled lives in towns and cities, while many keep their customs.
